passage:
The power had gone out in the last period, and the classroom was hot and dim. Hansa noticed Aadhya staring at her art sheet, lips pressed together. It was a lovely peacock, with 'Good, but colour outside lines' written in red.
Hansa almost said, 'That's nothing!' She wouldn't have minded one bit. Then she remembered how Mummy had asked her yesterday, 'What happened?' before saying anything else.
'What happened?' Hansa whispered.
'I worked on it all Sunday,' Aadhya said. 'Art is my one good thing.'
Hansa thought about that. Art wasn't her thing, but maths was. She'd feel awful if Sir wrote red lines on her maths.
'It's still the best peacock in class,' she said. 'Want help with the edges next time?'

qa.q: What was written in red on Aadhya's art sheet?
qa.a: 'Good, but colour outside lines.'

qa.q: Why did Hansa almost say 'That's nothing!'?
qa.a: Hansa wouldn't have minded such a comment herself, so at first she didn't see why Aadhya was upset.

qa.q: What turning point helped Hansa understand Aadhya?
qa.a: Remembering Mummy asking 'What happened?' made Hansa ask first, and hearing that art is Aadhya's one good thing let her compare it to her own maths.

qa.q: How might Aadhya feel when Hansa offers help with the edges?
qa.a: Aadhya may feel understood and supported rather than brushed off, since Hansa took the hurt seriously.

grounding: Shows a child starting to understand why a classmate is upset when she herself would not be, asking what happened and offering help, as an adult had modelled.

passage:
In the colony park after school, Lalremsiami sat on the swing but didn't swing. Urmila, nine, wanted to play catch. 'Come on!'
'I'm not in the mood.'
Urmila was puzzled. Ma'am had only changed the seating. Urmila didn't care where she sat. But her Papa, walking by with the vegetable bag, stopped. 'Siami, what happened, beta?'
'They moved me away from Grace. She's the only one I talk to in class.'
Urmila watched Papa ask and listen, and it clicked. For Siami, a seat wasn't just a seat.
'Tomorrow at lunch you can sit with me and Grace,' Urmila said. 'Every day, if you want.'
Siami pushed off with her feet, just a little.

qa.q: Who did Lalremsiami get moved away from?
qa.a: Grace, the only one Siami talks to in class.

qa.q: Why was Urmila puzzled at first?
qa.a: Urmila didn't care where she sat, so she couldn't see why a seating change would upset Lalremsiami.

qa.q: What turning point helped Urmila see things through Lalremsiami's eyes?
qa.a: Watching Papa ask what happened and listen made it click that a seat wasn't just a seat, so Urmila offered to sit together at lunch.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami feel when pushing off on the swing a little?
qa.a: Siami may feel a bit lighter and less alone, knowing Urmila understood.

grounding: Shows a child learning to see why another child is upset about something she would not mind, after an adult models asking and listening.

passage:
"Payal, why are you crying? It's just a drawing."
"It's not just a drawing, Yash. Ma'am put everyone's on the wall except mine."
"I wouldn't care. Mine's never on the wall."
"Well, I care!" Payal wiped her face.
Yash sat down on the step. He didn't get it. Then he remembered how he'd felt when he wasn't picked for the relay. "Is it like being left out?"
"Yes. Like everyone else counts and I don't."
"Oh." He thought. "What happened to it?"
"I think it fell behind the cupboard."
"Let's go and look. And if it's not there, we can ask Ma'am together."
Payal sniffed. "Okay."

qa.q: Where does Payal think her drawing went?
qa.a: Behind the cupboard.

qa.q: How did Yash come to understand Payal's upset?
qa.a: He remembered feeling left out when he wasn't picked for the relay, and saw she felt the same way.

qa.q: What did Yash do that showed growing empathy?
qa.a: He asked what happened and offered to look for the drawing and ask Ma'am together.

qa.q: How did Payal feel about her drawing not being on the wall?
qa.a: Payal felt left out and hurt, as if she didn't count.

grounding: Shows a child beginning to understand a friend's upset he wouldn't share, asking what happened and offering help.

passage: Last term my friend Aditi cried all through lunch because her Nani had moved back to the village. I didn't understand at first. My Dadi lives with us, and sometimes I'd like a bit less of her! But then I remembered how my mother always asks me, "What happened?" before saying anything else. So I asked Aditi. She told me her Nani used to plait her hair every morning and now nobody did. I'm Santosh, and I'm terrible at plaits. But the next day I brought her a hair clip shaped like a mango, and said she could call her Nani from our phone after school. She did. She laughed on the phone. I didn't feel what she felt, exactly. But I got it.

qa.q: What shape was the hair clip?
qa.a: A mango.

qa.q: How did Santosh feel at first about Aditi's crying?
qa.a: Santosh felt puzzled, not understanding why she was so sad, since Dadi at home could be a bit much.

qa.q: What helped Santosh understand and help Aditi?
qa.a: Copying the mother's habit of asking "What happened?" first, then offering a clip and a phone call to Nani.

qa.q: How did Aditi feel after the call with her Nani?
qa.a: Aditi felt happier, laughing on the phone.

grounding: Shows a child learning to understand a friend's sadness they wouldn't feel themselves, by asking what happened as an adult modelled.

passage: Class 4 note, Friday. Something small but lovely today. Bidisha was upset because her team lost the quiz, and Zainab, who doesn't care much about winning, first said, "It's only a quiz." Then she paused. On Monday I had asked the class to try "What happened?" before "It's only". Zainab asked, "Why does it matter so much to you?" Bidisha said her older brother had teased her all week that she'd lose. Zainab nodded slowly. "So it's not the quiz. It's your brother." She sat with Bidisha for the rest of break and helped her write down the answers she'd known. Next step: I will share this, without names, at Monday's circle time.

qa.q: Who had teased Bidisha all week?
qa.a: Her older brother.

qa.q: What did Zainab realise about Bidisha's upset?
qa.a: Zainab understood that Bidisha felt hurt by her brother's teasing, not just sad about losing.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped Zainab grow?
qa.a: Taught the class to ask "What happened?" first, and planned to share the example at circle time.

qa.q: How might Bidisha feel when Zainab sits with her?
qa.a: Bidisha probably feels understood and comforted.

grounding: Shows a child moving past her own view to understand why a friend is upset, supported by a teacher who modelled it.

passage:
Tuesday
Dear diary, today Mehak was really upset in art class because Ma'am put her painting on the board second, not first. I didn't get it. Second is still on the board! I would be happy.
But she was quiet all through lunch and didn't eat her paratha. So I asked her, "What happened?" like Mumma asks me.
She said her painting was of her Nani's house, and Nani passed away in the summer, so she wanted everyone to see it first.
Oh. So it wasn't about first and second at all. I told her it was the best house on the board and asked if she wanted to tell me about Nani. She talked for the whole break.
I still don't feel the way she does, but I think I understand now.
Akash

qa.q: Where did Ma'am put Mehak's painting?
qa.a: Ma'am put her painting on the board second, not first.

qa.q: What did Akash first think about Mehak being upset?
qa.a: Akash felt puzzled, because being second would have made Akash happy, so the upset didn't make sense at first.

qa.q: What did Akash try that could help other children understand a friend?
qa.a: Asking "What happened?" before judging, just as Mumma does, let Mehak explain the real reason and let Akash offer comfort.

qa.q: What would change for Mehak if nobody had asked her?
qa.a: She might have kept feeling sad and alone about her Nani, and her quiet lunch could have been mistaken for sulking over a place on the board.

grounding: Akash begins to understand why a friend is upset despite not feeling the same, asks what happened and helps, modelled on an adult.
